subtitle: Practice moving shared work forward when the people involved do not report to you. You will map who decides and who is affected, share credit fairly, make a case people can act on and handle disagreement with respect.
audience: For program leads, policy leads, project leads and anyone who moves work forward through people who do not report to them, in disability services or across the agency. It also suits people exploring leadership before they hold a title.

lessons.title: Knowing who decides and who is affected
objectives: Identify the decision owner, the people with a stake and the people most affected before you propose a change.
Distinguish the formal authority you were given from the personal authority you bring to a role.
Explain how the order in which you seek agreement shapes whose views count.
Draft a short map of a proposal you lead, including who is rarely asked and how you will reach them.
lessons.teaching:
Influence starts with knowing where the decision sits. Before you propose a change, find out who actually decides, who has a stake in the outcome and who will live with the result. These are often three different groups. A program lead may coordinate a waiver policy update while the decision belongs to a director, the work is done by county and lead agency staff, and the effects land on people receiving services and their families. Kathleen Pogue White's Person-Role-System briefing note defines authority simply as the right to do work. It says that stepping fully into your role takes a clarifying conversation with whoever authorized you. Use that conversation to learn what you may decide and what you may only recommend.

In White's framework, the distinction between two forms of authority helps clarify how you take up a role. She separates formal or delegated authority, which is passed to you by someone with more authority, from personal authority, which is the way you take up and carry out that role. She notes that personal authority is shaped by personality, culture and preference. FEMA's Leadership and Influence course draws a related line between influence that comes from position and interpersonal influence, which it says works best when you have no direct authority and need real buy-in. It also notes that influence runs in four directions: up to leaders, across to peers, down to people whose work you guide and outward to the public and partner communities. Notice your own habits, too. Your habits about when to speak, how hard to push and whom to ask first were learned somewhere. Examine whether those habits fit this task and the people involved; familiarity alone does not make a practice fair or effective.

The order of involvement matters as well as its reach: a familiar pattern is to seek agreement first from people already known to the project, people with formal authority and people easiest to reach. By the time anyone else hears the idea, its shape is set and their role is to react. The Casey Foundation's Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide makes a similar point: it is harder to bring new people in once an agenda, strategy and leadership are in place. The guide also separates engagement, which may only mean gathering input, from empowerment, where people help lead, decide and design. Ask early who is most affected and who is rarely asked, and be honest about which kind of involvement you can offer.

A simple map can draw on Minnesota's Equity Analysis Toolkit, which asks which groups a proposal may affect positively or negatively. The toolkit names equity and inclusion practitioners, HR leaders and accessibility coordinators among the partners to involve. Use those prompts to identify the decision owner, the decision needed and the people with a stake in the outcome. Include the people most affected, distinguishing what you know about their experience from questions that require further inquiry. For this planning exercise, map roles and groups without collecting unnecessary personal information. Keep authorized contact information and operational records in the appropriate systems under agency access and retention requirements.
lessons.keyPoint: Before you propose a change, know who decides, who has a stake and who lives with the result. Bring in the people most affected early, while their views can still shape the idea.
lessons.example: Practice case: Diane is a policy lead asked to simplify renewal paperwork for a disability waiver program. Her draft is ready. She plans to share it with her director, then with two county lead agency supervisors she trusts, then post it for comment. Luis, a self-advocate on an advisory group, tells her that people receiving services usually learn about paperwork changes when the new forms arrive in the mail. Her director wants a recommendation in three weeks.
lessons.question: What should Diane do next?
choices: Keep her plan, since the director decides and the comment period will give people receiving services a chance to respond to the draft.
Confirm with her director what she may change, then invite self-advocates and families to review the draft now, alongside the county supervisors.
Set the draft aside and ask the advisory group to rewrite the paperwork from the start, so that the people most affected lead the change.
feedback: The director does decide, but a comment period on a finished draft asks people to react rather than shape it. The people who fill out the forms are heard last, when changes are hardest to make.
This is the strongest choice. Diane clarifies her authority first, then brings in the people most affected while the draft can still change, and offers a role she can keep.

Inviting affected people to lead has real value, but promising a full rewrite may go beyond what Diane is authorized to do and miss the deadline. Clarifying the boundary first lets her offer a real role.
lessons.reflection: When you last proposed a change, whose agreement did you seek first and whose last? What did that order make easier, and for whom?
lessons.action: Choose one piece of work you are moving forward. Write down who decides, who has a stake and who is most affected. Note one group you have not yet heard from and one way you could reach them this month.

check.question: In this example, the proposal's scope is already fixed and the public can comment only on its details. What role does that offer the people most affected?
check.correct: A chance to react to an idea whose shape is already set, not to help shape it.
wrong: A role in leading and designing the change, since their comments can still alter it.
The same influence as the decision owner, since every comment is weighed equally.
check.feedback: Here the invitation comes after the scope has been fixed, so people can react to the proposal without sharing authority over its design. A comment process can support substantive changes when those changes are genuinely still open; explain what participants can influence.

lessons.title: Building trust and sharing credit across teams
objectives: Describe how reliability and fair credit build the trust that lets you lead without a title.
Identify moments in meetings and written work where the source of an idea gets lost.
Practice naming the source of an idea when you summarize, report or present shared work.
Plan one change to how your summaries and briefings attribute ideas to the people and teams who raised them.
lessons.teaching:
When colleagues do not report to you, trust, relevant expertise and a clear shared purpose can support cooperation. Their contribution may also be assigned work, with responsibilities and capacity limits that your project must respect. They are more likely to do it again when you are reliable: you follow through on what you said, you tell people early when something slips, and you let them know what happened with their input. Reliability sounds ordinary, but the rest of this course rests on it. A program lead who keeps small promises can ask for larger ones. FEMA's Leadership and Influence course calls this building alliances: you show you are a trustworthy ally, treat the other person as a valuable resource and make clear what you can do together. Knowing how the other team works helps too. The Center for Creative Leadership links inclusive leadership to its boundary spanning work and offers an illustration in which administrators shadowed doctors and doctors undertook administrative tasks. In DHS work, any observation or practice must stay within authorized duties, access permissions and required supervision.

Credit is part of trust, and it is not always shared evenly. In shared work, ideas travel. Someone raises a point in a small meeting, a colleague repeats it in a larger one, and by the time it reaches a summary or a briefing, the source is gone. The person who first raised it may be newer, quieter, joining by phone, thinking in a second language or simply not in the room. Repeated loss of credit can discourage contributions and make relevant expertise less visible. It does not establish how any particular colleague will respond. No one has to intend it for the pattern to take hold.

Fair credit is a fairness practice, not a courtesy. Deloitte's report on the six signature traits of inclusive leadership describes fairness in three parts: fair outcomes, fair processes and clear communication with the people affected. It also describes inclusive leaders bringing every team member into discussion and asking follow-up questions. The report is consulting research built on interviews and a small pilot, not a controlled study, but the practice it points to is useful. For ordinary shared work, accurate attribution helps people understand where an idea came from. Check the contributor's preference and any confidentiality limits before identifying someone publicly; appropriate team attribution can also recognize collaborative work.

Amplifying an overlooked contribution is a skill you can practice in any role. When a point is passed over, return to it and name who raised it. When you write a summary, attribute ideas to the people or teams who offered them. When you brief a leader, say whose analysis it was, and invite that person to present when you can. Ask yourself whose ideas get credited in your project and how you would know. Then look at your own last few documents. Your summaries provide one source of evidence, but may omit contributions made elsewhere. Ask about those gaps without turning this exercise into an unauthorized personnel evaluation.
lessons.keyPoint: Reliability and accurate credit can support trust across teams. Recognize the source of an idea when you use it, while respecting appropriate attribution, confidentiality and the contributor's preferences.
lessons.example: Practice case: Farah leads a project to speed up interpreter requests across three teams in a human services agency. In an early working session, Oluwaseun, a program consultant who joins by phone, suggested routing all requests through one shared calendar. Two weeks later, a manager from another team presented the same idea at the steering meeting as his team's proposal, and leaders liked it. Farah is now writing the project summary for the deputy director. Oluwaseun has agreed to be named in the project summary, and the attribution does not reveal protected information.
lessons.question: How should Farah handle the summary?
choices: Write the summary around the proposal and leave all names out, since what matters most to the deputy director is that the idea moves forward.
Speak privately with the manager about what happened and ask him to correct the record with leaders before she sends anything.
Tell the manager how she will describe the idea, then note in the summary that it came from Oluwaseun's session and thank his team for advancing it.
feedback: Leaving names out feels neutral, but it lets the most recent speaker keep the credit. Oluwaseun's work stays invisible, and the summary does not accurately recognize his contribution.
A private word may help later, but it puts the fix on someone else and delays an accurate record. Farah controls her own summary and can make it accurate now without blaming anyone.
This is the strongest choice. Farah makes the record accurate without surprising anyone, gives Oluwaseun visible credit and recognizes the other team's support without assuming harm.
lessons.reflection: Think of a time your idea was credited to someone else, or the reverse. What made it happen, and what would have kept the record accurate?
lessons.action: Look at the last two summaries, notes or briefings you wrote for shared work. Check whether each key idea is credited to the person or team who raised it, and add that attribution to the next one you write.

check.question: For an ordinary project idea whose contributor welcomes attribution and whose identity may be shared, which practice best reflects fair credit?
check.correct: Naming who raised an idea at the point it is used, in meetings, notes and briefings.
wrong: Leaving every name out of summaries so that no one person gets more credit than another.
Thanking everyone on the project equally at the end, once the final decision is made.
check.feedback: In this example, attribution can travel with the idea because naming the contributor is appropriate. General thanks alone do not identify the contribution; privacy requirements and the contributor's preferences still matter in other settings.

lessons.title: Making a case that people can act on
objectives: Build a case for a proposal around shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed.
Adapt the same case for audiences with different responsibilities and concerns.
Offer more than one way for people to respond, so support does not depend on speaking up in one meeting.
Compare how a habit of making a case looks at three points on the intercultural development continuum.
lessons.teaching:
A good case tells people what to do, not only what to think. The Casey Foundation's Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide describes a framing sequence: the shared values at stake, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed. It was written for conversations about race equity, and this course adapts the sequence as a planning aid for shared-work proposals. Distinguish an established cause from a hypothesis when the available evidence does not yet explain the problem. A director may need the decision and its risks. A lead agency partner may need to know what changes in their workload. A provider may need the timeline. A self-advocate may want to know what improves for people and how to shape it. The values and facts stay the same; the emphasis changes.

Offer more than one way to take part. A proposal that can only be supported or challenged out loud, in one meeting, favors people who are comfortable speaking quickly in a group. Share material ahead of time in plain language and accessible formats. Invite written comments, short one-on-one conversations and small group discussions as well as the meeting itself. Give people time to check with their own teams. Then check whether it worked: who responded, through which route, and who has not responded at all.

Communication styles differ, and silence is not the same as agreement. People and teams vary in how directly they disagree, whether they raise concerns in public or in private, how much context they expect before a request and how long they need to consult before they commit. Minnesota's Equity Analysis Toolkit describes intercultural competence as being able to see from another cultural point of view and change how you act to fit both differences and what people share. Deloitte's report describes a similar habit in inclusive leaders: changing style when the situation calls for it while staying authentic.

The intercultural development continuum helps you see this skill as a practice that grows. IDI, LLC describes five orientations on its Intercultural Development Continuum: Denial, Polarization, Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. A Minimization habit sounds like this: I present every proposal the same way, because a good case speaks for itself. An Acceptance habit notices that people respond differently and that a quiet room may hold real doubts. An Adaptation habit changes the process, for example by sending a plain summary first, holding follow-up conversations and inviting written concerns. These are course illustrations, not a way to assess an individual's orientation from one behavior. A change of communication channel alone does not establish intercultural Adaptation. Ask which habits shape your own way of making a case.
lessons.keyPoint: Frame the case around shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed. Then offer several ways to respond, because a quiet room is not the same as agreement.
lessons.example: Practice case: Yuki is a program lead in disability services. She is proposing a shared checklist that licensing staff and providers would use before site visits. At a large provider meeting, the licensing manager supports it, but most provider representatives say nothing. Afterward, Greg, who runs two small group homes, emails her that smaller agencies have concerns they did not want to raise in front of the licensing team.
lessons.question: What should Yuki do next?
choices: Send a short plain-language summary, offer brief calls and a written comment option, and share back what she hears before any decision.
Move ahead with the checklist, since the licensing manager supports it and every provider had a fair chance to object during the meeting itself.
Hold a second large meeting and ask each provider in turn to state a view aloud, so that every voice is heard and recorded.
feedback: This is the strongest choice. Yuki adapts the process to how concerns are actually being raised, offers additional routes for smaller providers to raise concerns and closes the loop before a decision.
Moving ahead is tempting when the licensing area supports the idea, but silence in front of a regulator may hold real doubts. Concerns that go unheard tend to return later as problems.
Asking each person aloud aims at fairness, but it repeats the setting where people chose not to speak, in front of the licensing team. It may produce answers that are not candid.
lessons.reflection: What do you usually take as a sign that people agree with you? Where did you learn to read agreement that way, and when has it misled you?
lessons.action: Take a proposal you are working on and write it in five short lines: the shared value, the problem, the cause, the solution and the action needed. Then add two ways, besides a meeting, that people could respond.

check.question: In the course's simplified continuum illustration, which example represents adapting the process after considering different perspectives and response needs?
check.correct: Changing the process, such as sending a plain summary first and inviting written concerns.
wrong: Presenting the case the same way to everyone, because a strong case speaks for itself.
Noticing that people respond differently and that a quiet room may hold real doubts.
check.feedback: The illustration links changing the process to Adaptation, while noticing difference alone illustrates Acceptance. These examples support reflection; they do not establish an individual's orientation, and accessibility measures should be available regardless of an assessment.

lessons.title: When agreement does not come
objectives: Plan a transparent escalation of an ordinary project disagreement while preserving protected and urgent reporting routes.
Distinguish a disagreement about the work from a concern that belongs with Human Resources or the equal opportunity office.
Describe how to implement a lawful, authorized decision you did not prefer while keeping its reasons and review conditions visible.
Write a short decision note that records the decision, its reasons and what would prompt a second look.
lessons.teaching:
Disagreement is normal when you lead without a title. People on different teams have different duties, pressures and evidence, and some disagreements cannot be settled by more persuasion. For an ordinary project disagreement, try to understand the other view well enough to state it fairly. This conversation is not a prerequisite for an urgent escalation or a protected report. Ask what evidence each side has, and what an equity analysis would show about who benefits and who carries the burden. Sometimes the disagreement turns out to rest on a fact you can check together.

For ordinary differences over project options, involve the decision owner transparently and present both views where practicable. White's Person-Role-System briefing note suggests that when you reach the edge of your authority, the next step is a negotiation with the person who authorized the work, built on the case for what you need. In practice, tell the colleague you disagree with that you plan to bring the question to the decision owner, and invite them to come or to send their view. Try: "We still see this differently. I plan to bring both options to the decision owner this week. Would you like to present yours, or send it with mine?" Present both positions fairly, with the evidence behind each and the effects on the people most affected. Transparent handling can support working relationships, but it does not guarantee agreement. Do not notify a colleague first when that would compromise a protected report, confidential advice or an appropriate response to urgent risk.

Possible discrimination, harassment, retaliation, accommodation requests and labor concerns require the designated agency process rather than an informal project debate. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Other employees should use the applicable agency reporting route promptly; they need not investigate or prove an allegation before reporting it. Route possible accommodation requests to the appropriate decision-maker under MMB Policy 1433, recognizing that a request does not need special terminology. Consult HR, labor relations, the equal opportunity office or counsel according to the issue and your role. These referrals do not erase related operational barriers, records duties or required follow-up within the project; share sensitive details only with authorized recipients.

Implementing a lawful, authorized decision you did not prefer can be part of collaborative leadership. White's framework describes contributing to a collective result without retaining sole control; it does not require unconditional obedience. Use the appropriate reporting, legal or safety route when a decision raises those concerns. Minnesota Statutes section 181.932 protects specified reports and refusals under its stated conditions, which should not be replaced by this course's collaboration advice. For an ordinary decision within your responsibilities, explain the outcome honestly, record its reasons and specify what new evidence or effects would prompt review. Preserve that record under agency requirements, then examine what happened for the people affected.
lessons.keyPoint: For an ordinary project disagreement, bring the decision owner both views and their evidence. Preserve protected and urgent reporting routes, then implement lawful decisions within your responsibilities and review their effects.
lessons.example: Practice case: Brian is a project lead redesigning how a human services agency tells people about appointment changes. He wants text reminders paired with phone calls, because older adults and people who use relay services told him texts alone get missed. Valentina, who manages the contact center, wants texts only to control costs and has said she will not change her view. Ifeoma, the deputy director, decides next week. This is an ordinary choice between authorized reminder options; no urgent safety issue, protected complaint or confidential reporting concern is involved.
lessons.question: What should Brian do now?
choices: Let the decision go ahead and raise his concerns afterward if the texts-only approach causes problems, since Valentina's team runs the center.
Tell Valentina he will bring both options to Ifeoma, invite her to present her case alongside his, and share what affected people told him.
Email Ifeoma privately with his evidence before the meeting, so she hears from the people affected before she hears the cost argument.
feedback: Waiting avoids conflict, but it lets the decision go forward without evidence from the people most affected. Raising problems afterward is harder for them and for Brian.

This is the strongest choice. Brian escalates openly, gives Ifeoma both cases and the evidence from people affected, and gives Valentina an opportunity to explain her position without assuming that disagreement will disappear.

In this ordinary project disagreement, an unexplained private approach gives the decision owner only one side when a joint presentation is available. Confidential advice, protected reports and urgent escalation may require a different route.
lessons.reflection: Think of a decision at work that you disagreed with. How did you respond once it was made, and what would you keep or change about that next time?
lessons.action: Choose an ordinary shared-work decision to map this week: who decides, who is affected and whose ideas your summary credits. Explain how you would present both views of a project disagreement, preserving protected reporting routes and confidentiality.

check.question: A project colleague raises possible disability discrimination. Which response correctly separates the complaint process from an informal project debate, alongside any reporting duties you hold?
check.correct: Help the colleague reach Human Resources or the equal opportunity office, and keep it apart from the project.
wrong: Raise it with the decision owner as part of the project disagreement, so that it is heard and settled quickly.
Look into what happened yourself first, so you can tell the decision owner whether it holds up.
check.feedback: Use the designated complaint route rather than investigating or resolving the allegation through the project. Managers and supervisors must report immediately under MMB Policy 1436. Keeping the complaint process separate does not remove operational responsibilities or authorize ignoring related barriers.

cards.back: The person or area with the authority to make the final call on a proposal. Knowing who it is, and what they need to decide, comes before building support.
Formal authority is delegated by someone with more authority. Personal authority is how you take up and carry out that role, shaped by personality, culture and preference.

Influence that rests on trust rather than position: I am a trustworthy ally, you are a valuable resource and we can do this together. It works best when you have no direct authority and need real buy-in.
Engagement may mean gathering input. Empowerment means people help lead, decide and design. Be honest about which one you are offering before you invite people in.
Returning to an overlooked idea and accurately recognizing its source, using individual or team attribution appropriate to the contribution, the person's preferences and confidentiality requirements.

For an ordinary project disagreement, bringing the decision owner both views and their evidence transparently. Protected reports, confidential advice and urgent concerns may require a different route.

aid.heading: Before you propose a change
items: Confirm with whoever authorized the work what you may decide and what you may only recommend.
Write down who decides, who has a stake and who is most affected, looking up, across, down and outside the agency.
Name who is rarely asked, what you know of their experience and how you will reach them early.
Decide honestly whether you are offering a chance to give input or a role in shaping the result.

aid.heading: While you build support
items: Keep small promises, and say early when something will slip.
Attribute ideas accurately, checking whether individual or team credit is appropriate and whether the contributor may be named.
Frame the case: shared values, the problem, its cause, the solution and the action needed.
Offer written, one-on-one and small group ways to respond as well as the meeting.
Check who responded, through which route, and who has not responded at all.

aid.heading: When agreement does not come
items: State the other view fairly, and look for facts you could check together.
For an ordinary project disagreement, tell the colleague you will bring both views to the decision owner; preserve protected and urgent reporting routes.
Try: "We still see this differently. I will bring both options to the decision owner this week. Will you present yours, or send it with mine?"
Use designated complaint, accommodation and labor processes; managers and supervisors must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination under MMB Policy 1436.
Implement lawful, authorized decisions within your duties, preserve the reasons and review conditions, and use appropriate reporting or advice routes for unresolved legal or safety concerns.
Later, ask what happened, for whom, and what you will keep, change or stop.

sources.title: Kathleen Pogue White — Person-Role-System Framework Briefing Note (2013), hosted copy
sources.note: Supports authority as the right to do work, formal versus personal authority shaped by culture, the clarifying conversation and negotiation at the edge of authority, and bearing the loss of sole agency. A consultant's framework for results-based leadership work, not a research study.

sources.title: Annie E. Casey Foundation — Race Equity and Inclusion Action Guide: Embracing Equity, 7 Steps (2014)
sources.note: Supports the points that new people are harder to bring in once an agenda is set, the engagement and empowerment distinction, and the five-part framing sequence. Written for race equity work in 2014; applied here more broadly.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget, Office of Inclusion — State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit: A Quick Guide
sources.note: Supports the prompt about which groups a proposal may affect, the partners it names, including HR leaders and accessibility coordinators, and its description of intercultural competence. Does not say when use is required.

sources.title: Dillon, B. and Bourke, J. — The six signature traits of inclusive leadership: Thriving in a diverse new world, Deloitte University Press (2016)
sources.note: Supports fairness in outcomes, processes and communication, bringing every team member into discussion, and changing style while staying authentic. 2016 consulting research from interviews in six countries and a small pilot, mostly private sector.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Supports the names and order of the five orientations IDI, LLC describes, used here only to describe habits of making a case at Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation. Nothing in this course assesses anyone.

sources.title: FEMA Emergency Management Institute — IS-240.B Leadership and Influence, Student Manual (February 2014)
sources.note: Adapted from Lesson 5: influence from position versus interpersonal influence, the four directions of influence, and the ally elements of building alliances. Federal public domain material. The current IS-240.c (2021) may differ, and its emergency management examples are not used.

sources.title: Dunne-Moses, Dawkins, Futch Ehrlich, Clerkin and Crittle — The Research Foundations for REAL: A Framework for Leadership Action in Equity, Diversity & Inclusion, Center for Creative Leadership (2023)
sources.note: Supports the link between inclusive leadership and boundary spanning, and the shadowing and task-swap example, paraphrased. Copyrighted; ideas only. The paper does not say whether its client examples are real or composite, and reports no validation study.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1436, Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited (revised 2024)
sources.note: Supports examples of protected-class harassment including deliberate misgendering and name mispronunciation, supervisor duty to report immediately, and the retaliation prohibition.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — HR/LR Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodation
sources.note: Supports recognizing requests without special wording, promptly forwarding them to the appropriate decision maker, notifying the person who decides and following agency procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 181.932 — Disclosure of information by employees
sources.note: Protects specified reporting and refusal activities under statutory conditions. Collaborative leadership advice does not replace those protections or legal guidance.
